summary: In this episode, Fathers Andrew Stephen Damick and Stephen De Young address the Orthodox Christian practice of patron saints, defending it against charges of paganism and lack of biblical basis. They argue that the Bible reflects a robust spiritual reality where angelic beings are assigned to elements of nature, peoples, and persons, and that human saints, through theosis, come to fill the vacancies left by fallen angels. The discussion traces this theme from the Old Testament divine council, through the New Testament and early church, to contemporary application in spiritual warfare and the transformation of communities.

entities.title: Philo of Alexandria
entities.summary: First-century Jewish philosopher who wrote about the divine administration and the subordinate role of heavenly bodies as 'gods' under the one supreme God.

entities.title: Saint John Chrysostom
entities.summary: Major Church Father quoted on how people become like demons through sin, not through violent death.

entities.title: Saint Demetrius
entities.summary: Patron saint of Thessaloniki, who replaced Aphrodite as the spirit of the city through the people's realignment with Christ.

entities.title: Aphrodite
entities.summary: Pagan goddess formerly associated with Thessaloniki, replaced by Saint Demetrius as the city's patron.

entities.title: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
entities.summary: 19th-century German philosopher whose view of history as the unfolding of the Holy Spirit influenced liberal theology.

entities.title: Saint Augustine
entities.summary: Church Father and saint, noted for his life and confessions, despite some theological errors that he himself retracted.

entities.title: Arius
entities.summary: Heretic who refused correction from the Church, leading to his condemnation at the Council of Nicaea.

concepts.title: Patron Saints
concepts.summary: The practice of having particular saints as patrons for individuals, places, churches, and groups, rooted in the biblical and early Christian understanding of holy ones (angels and humans) assigned to guide and intercede.

concepts.title: Divine Council
concepts.summary: The biblical and Second Temple Jewish concept of a council of divine beings (angels, 'gods') who serve as administrators under God, governing creation and nations. This council is renewed in Christ, with human saints joining it.

concepts.title: Theosis (Deification)
concepts.summary: The process of becoming like God through participation in His divine life, aligning one's will with God's, and ultimately becoming 'equal to the angels' and sharing in God's stewardship of creation.

concepts.title: Spirit as Phenomenological
concepts.summary: Understanding 'spirit' not as a material or metaphysical entity but as a relational and experiential reality—how a being (angelic or human) relates to and influences a group, place, or person.

concepts.title: Koinonia (Participation)
concepts.summary: The Greek term for fellowship/participation, used to describe the synergistic relationship between humans and spiritual beings (God, angels, demons) through alignment of wills and activities.

concepts.title: Holy Tradition
concepts.summary: The life of the Holy Spirit in the Church, understood as the historical instances where humans synergized with the Holy Spirit, which serve as authoritative guides for the Church.

concepts.title: Liberal Theology
concepts.summary: A post-Enlightenment theological approach that sees history as progressing toward a pinnacle (often the present culture) and interprets that development as the work of the Holy Spirit, leading to a rejection of tradition.

claims.text: The practice of patron saints is not thinly veiled paganism; it is rooted in the biblical understanding of holy ones (angels and humans) assigned to guide and intercede, and it is distinct from polytheism because these beings are created and subordinate to God.
Human saints in glory fill the vacancies left by fallen angelic beings, becoming 'equal to the angels' and participating in the divine council, as seen in Scripture and church tradition.
Salvation is not merely about escaping hell but about becoming part of the divine council, sharing in God's stewardship of creation, and being co-enthroned with Christ.
A heretic is not simply someone who is wrong, but someone who, after being corrected by the Church, refuses to repent and persists in teaching error, often leading to schism.

Liberal theology, by viewing the present culture as the apex of history and the work of the Holy Spirit, is inherently chauvinist, racist, and colonial, as it dismisses other cultures and traditions as backward.

scriptural_links.summary: Used to show that God allotted the sun, moon, and stars (heavenly host) to the nations, indicating angelic beings assigned to peoples.
Interpreted as God judging the 'gods' (angelic beings) who failed to administer justice, and as a prophecy of Christ's authority over the nations.
Christ's declaration that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Him, fulfilling Psalm 82 and commissioning the apostles to make disciples of all nations.
Jesus says that those who are sons of the resurrection are equal to the angels, supporting the idea that glorified humans share in angelic roles.
Baptism for the dead is interpreted as a patron relationship, where living believers act on behalf of departed saints, reflecting the practice of taking a saint's name.
